title: The autumn equinox
hook: balance again, and the light begins to shorten

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ripe olive, falling in its season and thanking the tree. Your line was in season. What did you taste that was ripe right now? Day six hundred seventy-one.

It shows up first at dinner. In August, dinner was eaten in daylight. Now the kitchen light is on before the pasta's done. The mornings are cooler. The trees on your street have a few yellow leaves, like the first gray hairs. Back in the spring, on the porch, we stood at the equinox and watched the light begin to win. Today the scale balances again, day and night nearly even. But this time, from here, in the north, the dark grows. The autumn equinox: the same balance, facing the other way.
screen: `THE KITCHEN LIGHT, ON EARLIER.` → `A FEW YELLOW LEAVES.` → `THE SAME BALANCE, FACING THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. Astronomically, it's the mirror of spring: the sun crosses the equator heading south, and the northern days grow shorter than the nights. Same balance, different direction. Some people feel it in their mood, a slight heaviness as evenings close in. That's real, and it's worth being gentle with. Second, Seneca in autumn. In his twelfth letter, he visits his country house and grumbles to the caretaker that the old plane trees look neglected. The caretaker says he's doing all he can; the trees are just old. Then Seneca remembers: he planted them himself. The trees are simply his age. And then the letter turns: he says we should welcome and love old age, because it is full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit, he says, is most welcome when it's almost over. Third, the Stoic view of turnings. For Seneca and Marcus, nature's cycles aren't something going wrong. Seasons turn, people age, the light comes and goes, and all of it belongs to the same whole. That doesn't mean you have to like the shorter days. It means you can stop treating them as a mistake. Fourth, what autumn offers. The best light of the year, some say: low, gold, long shadows. Harvest. A slower pace. The turning isn't only loss. It's a different kind of day, with its own gifts, the way the later part of a life has its own. Dusk shows it plainly, when day and night meet in the same sky.
screen: `THE MIRROR OF SPRING.` · `SENECA'S OLD PLANE TREES.` · `TURNINGS AREN'T MISTAKES.` · `A DIFFERENT DAY, WITH ITS OWN GIFTS.` · then, large: `THE TURNING.`

segments.voice: If it's near evening, step outside, or to a window, and watch the light go. If it's earlier, picture a dusk you remember. Notice the colors as the day drains out of the sky. The sounds changing. The air cooling. Don't hurry it, and don't hold on to it. Let the day turn into evening while you watch. If a feeling of loss comes, let it be there. If a feeling of rest comes, let that be there too. The bell holds the time.
Autumn equinox, when day and night return to balance but the light begins to shorten, a turning with its own gifts. Today's word.
Your line: the turning. Take a short walk at dusk this evening, and notice one thing the turning season gives rather than takes. Day six hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Many cultures hold harvest festivals around the autumn equinox; some readers of the Stoics mark it with a dusk walk and a reflection on the seasons of life.

fork.setup: you're Seneca, scolding your caretaker about neglected old trees. he says they're just old. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Seneca sees that he's as old as the trees, and turns the letter into praise of old age.
